title: "I Still Have Twelve Ships"
text:
In 1597 Japan invaded Korea for the second time. The Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin, who had defeated the Japanese at sea during the first invasion, had been falsely accused, arrested, tortured and demoted to the rank of a common soldier. His replacement, Won Gyun, led the Korean fleet to disaster at Chilcheollyang in the summer of 1597. Almost the entire fleet was destroyed.

The court hastily restored Yi to command. He found only about a dozen warships left. King Seonjo, judging the navy finished, suggested that Yi abandon the sea and join the land forces. Yi replied in a report to the court that he still had twelve ships, and that as long as he lived, the enemy would not dare to look down on Korea's navy.

In October 1597, with thirteen ships, he met a Japanese fleet of more than a hundred and thirty warships at the Myeongnyang Strait, a narrow channel with violent tidal currents. He chose the place because the strait limited how many enemy ships could engage at once. Yi's flagship held the line almost alone at first. By the end of the day dozens of Japanese ships had been sunk or damaged, and Yi had lost none.
lesson: Do not let what you have lost define you. Count what you still have, choose ground where it counts, and commit.
location: Myeongnyang Strait, South Jeolla (modern South Korea)
source: Yi Sun-sin, War Diary (Nanjung Ilgi); Annals of the Joseon Dynasty; Yi Bun, Biography of Yi Sun-sin
caveat: Japanese losses at Myeongnyang are uncertain, and Korean and Japanese sources give different figures.
